newsitem.title: USA: U.S. in inflationary danger zone says Fed's Yellen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. in inflationary danger zone says Fed's Yellen.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
The economy has entered an inflationary danger zone and the Federal Reserve must be alert to the risk that could pose to continued economic expansion, a senior central banker said Tuesday.
"We're in an inflationary danger zone," Fed Gov. Janet Yellen said in an interview. "There's definitely a chance inflation will rise."
She stressed that there were uncertainties regarding the economy and that the outlook for inflation and growth were not completely clear.
"The evidence isn't utterly definitive we're going to see inflation rise," Yellen said.

Her cautious comments suggested that she might be willing to support a small, quarter percentage point rise in short-term interest rates at the Fed's next policy-making meeting on Sept. 24 to help ensure against higher inflation.

Such a move, if it occurred, would be the first rate increase by the central bank in about 1-1/2 years and would be designed to head off a rise in inflation that could jeopardise the 5-1/2-year-old economic expansion.
"We have to be quite careful," Yellen said. "We've had a long expansion here. I'm anxious to see that maintained."
She said she had been surprised by the strength of the economy so far this year.

The economy grew at a 4.8 percent annualized pace in the second quarter -- its quickest rate in two years and about twice as fast as most economists reckon it can expand on a long-term basis without fanning inflation.
Although Yellen expects growth to ebb in the coming months, she said the timing and extent of the slowdown remained uncertain.
"The momentum of demand is likely to subside going forward," Yellen said. "How much and when I can't tell you for sure."

The latest sign of the economy's strength came last Friday with news that the unemployment rate fell to 5.1 percent in August, its lowest level in nearly 7-1/2 years, as the economy created 250,000 jobs.
"Employment growth has been very strong," Yellen said. "You have quite tight labour markets at this point."
So far, though, there is no sign of a wage-driven rise in inflation.
"The underlying inflation trend is stable or declining, depending on what (indicator) you choose to focus on," Yellen said.
Wages and salaries have begun to pick up, but the growth of overall worker compensation, which includes benefits as well and which determines companies' labour costs, has remained moderate, she said.
"We're beginning to see a little bit of an increase in the growth of compensation," she said. "But it's hard to say that's a sign that inflation must rise."

Corporate earnings have been "extremely strong" and profit margins have held up very well, Yellen said. Companies seem confident they can keep costs down and continue to complain of difficulties in raising prices.
Neverthless, the Fed policymaker said the central bank needed to be forward-looking in setting interest rate policy.

When the unemployment rate was hovering around 5-1/2 percent earlier this year and in 1995, Yellen was a vocal advocate of allowing that to continue, despite fears of some Fed officials that it showed the economy was overheating.
But now, in Yellen's words, the labour market has tightened "another notch" with the drop in the jobless rate toward 5 percent.

"There is the danger that if we reach for the marginal gain (in employment) and we're wrong, we could jeopardise the expansion that we've had," she said. "Continuing a growth path that is sustainable seems to me what our priority should be."
But that does not mean deciding the course of interest rates is easy now. Yellen described the task as a difficult balancing of the risks and benefits.

According to Yellen, the Fed faces two key questions -- what is the future course of the economy and has the economy already overshot its long-term potential. The answer to neither is completely clear.

She ticked off a variety of reasons to expect economic growth to slow in the months ahead. The housing market is likely to weaken under the impact of higher interest rates. Government spending should slow from recent very strong levels, which were a "bit of a mystery."
Consumer spending started off the quarter weak, but August car sales looked strong. "It's hard to get a reading at this point," Yellen said.
